Implementation lives in `emitter/out/Booking_M2/all_public/src/test/java/com/testgen/booking/PublicTests.java`.

| 1   | TC01 — POST registerPath() with a fresh email returns 2xx and a JWT token                                                                                                                               | `public`, `features_m2` | `POST registerPath()` | The §S1-F1 register endpoint must persist a brand-new User account to PostgreSQL and respond with HTTP 2xx plus a body containing a non-blank JWT `token` and a positive `expiresIn` (in milliseconds). Per spec the response shape is `{ "token": "...", "expiresIn": ... }` — no `id` field is returned; chained tests resolve the new user's id from the JWT (`uidFromJwt()`) or via login. | 1) Build a JSON register body with a `nonce()`-suffixed email (e.g., `tc01_<nonce>@grader.testgen.io`), fixed name `"TC01 User"`, a fresh phone string, and a strong password (`TestPwd!2026`).<br>2) POST `/api/users/register` with `Content-Type: application/json` and that body.<br>3) Assert HTTP status is in the 2xx range via `assert2xx`.<br>4) Parse the response body as JSON.<br>5) Assert `token` is non-null and a non-blank string.<br>6) Assert `expiresIn` is present and a positive numeric value. | • HTTP status 200..299<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Bug it catches:** Validation rejects a perfectly-valid payload (`@NotBlank` or `@Email` mis-configured), or the persistence path throws and the exception leaks as 5xx (BCrypt encoder not wired, schema column missing, transaction not committing).<br>• Body has non-null `token` field<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Bug it catches:** Controller returns `{"id":42}` or an empty body instead of the spec-defined `{token, expiresIn}` envelope — clients have no JWT to authenticate subsequent calls.<br>• `token` is a non-blank string<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Bug it catches:** JWT signing wired but emits `""` on a code path (e.g., the secret is read as null and the signer silently produces an empty header.payload.signature triple) — auth filter would later reject every request with that token.<br>• `expiresIn` present and > 0<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Bug it catches:** `expiresIn` returned as `0` or omitted — clients have no TTL to manage refresh; usually means the JWT-config Singleton's expiration property was never read.

Checks that the token is exactly three dot-separated segments (`header.payload.signature`) — the canonical compact-serialisation format defined by RFC 7519. Maps to spec S1-F11 (login / token issuance). Common bugs: login issues a plain UUID or opaque string instead of a JWT; the token key in the response body is named differently (e.g., `accessToken`); the token value is blank or null; or the JWT is missing one segment (only two parts, no signature). The setup registers a fresh user first so the test is fully self-contained and does not rely on pre-seeded data.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | 1) Register a fresh user with `"email":"tc02_<nonce>@grader.testgen.io"` and `"password":"TestPwd!2026"`. assert `token` field exists and is non-null.<br>6) Assert `token` is a non-blank string.<br>7) Split `token` on `.` and assert exactly 3 segments.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | • Login status 200..299<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: login endpoint not mapped (404) or the auth filter accidentally covers the login path itself, blocking it with 401.<br>• Body has non-blank `token` field<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: response body uses a different key (`accessToken`, `jwt`, `bearerToken`) instead of `token`; | 3   | TC03 — Read own user profile with valid JWT (happy path)                                                  | `public`, `updated_crud`                                                              | `POST registerPath()` (setup), `POST loginPath()` (setup), `GET crudReadPath("User")`                                                                | Validates the full authentication chain end-to-end: the JWT issued by login must be accepted by Spring Security's `OncePerRequestFilter`, the principal extracted from the token must match the path variable `{id}`, and `GET /api/users/{id}` must return the correct user row as a JSON object. Maps to spec S1-F7 (get user by id, with ownership). Tagged `updated_crud` because this CRUD endpoint was updated in M2 to require auth (M1 had no auth). Common bugs: auth filter is registered only on `/api/auth/**`, leaving `/api/users/**` unprotected or completely broken; the filter parses the JWT but does not call `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication()`, causing the ownership check to NPE; or the controller returns 403 even for the legitimate owner due to an inverted ownership comparison. Strict `2xx` — **not** the `2xx OR 404` escape — because we registered this exact user moments before; a 404 here is a real persistence or filter-chain bug. | 1) Register a fresh user (`tc03_<nonce>@grader.testgen.io`). Assert 2xx. Extract `uid` by decoding the JWT `token` field and reading the `sub` claim as a Long.<br>2) Login with the same credentials. Assert 2xx. Capture `token`.<br>3) `GET /api/users/<uid>` with header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.<br>4) Assert status is 200–299 (strict — no 404 escape).<br>5) Parse response body; assert it is a JSON object (not an array or primitive).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | • GET status 200..299 (strict, **not** the `2xx OR 404` escape)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: JWT filter fails to extract the principal and throws NPE/500; or the filter parses claims but does not write to `SecurityContextHolder`, leaving the controller with an anonymous principal that triggers 401 or 403 even for the legitimate owner.<br>• Response body parses as a JSON object<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: controller returns an empty body (204 No Content), a JSON array (`[]`), or a plain string instead of the user entity object; Jackson serialisation error swallowed as an empty response.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

Primary bugs caught: `@Column(unique=true)` missing on `User.email` causes the second registration to succeed silently (2xx); an uncaught `DataIntegrityViolationException` from JPA propagates as a 5xx; or a catch block re-throws the exception with a 5xx-range custom status. Strict `4xx` range assertion (not just "not-2xx") is chosen because the spec requires a client-error response — a 5xx indicates a separate crash bug, not a handled duplicate-email error.                                                                                                                                                                                                             | 1) Build payload with `"email":"tc04_<nonce>@grader.testgen.io"` and valid password/phone.<br>2) `POST /api/auth/register` — assert 2xx (precondition: verifies the email is fresh).<br>3) `POST /api/auth/register` **again** with the **same email** but a different name/phone.<br>4) Parse the second response status.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | • First register status 200..299<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: the test pre-condition itself failed — something wrong with the register endpoint before the duplicate attempt (validation too strict, or server crashed).<br>• Second register status 400..499 (strict — must be a client error)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: `@Column(unique=true)` missing on `User.email` — second register creates a duplicate row silently (2xx); or the constraint violation leaks as unhandled `DataIntegrityViolationException` (5xx).<br>• NOT 5xx (no server crash on the duplicate)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: duplicate key exception propagating from JPA through the service as an uncaught runtime exception, producing a 500 Internal Server Error.<br>• NOT 2xx (uniqueness must be enforced)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: email uniqueness constraint missing entirely; two users can share the same email address.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| 5   | TC05 — Login with wrong password returns 401 (negative path)                                              | `public`, `features_m2`                                                               | `POST registerPath()` (setup), `POST loginPath()`                                                                                                    | The login endpoint must authenticate the supplied password against the stored BCrypt hash and reject a mismatch with exactly `401 Unauthorized`. Maps to spec S1-F11 (authentication). The assertion ladder is ordered from most-dangerous to most-pedantic bug: a 2xx means password checking was skipped entirely (critical security hole); a 5xx means an unhandled exception leaked; a 404 means the controller leaks whether an email exists (OWASP user-enumeration anti-pattern — when an *existing* user enters the wrong password, the response must be 401, not 404); a 403 is structurally wrong because login is the act of *obtaining* permissions, not *exercising* them. Both `"TestPwd!2026"` and `"WrongPwd!2026"` differ in prefix and length so BCrypt cannot accidentally match.                                                                                                                                                                                              | 1) Register a fresh user with `"email":"tc05_<nonce>@grader.testgen.io"` and `"password":"TestPwd!2026"`. Assert 2xx.<br>2) Build login body with the **same email** but `"password":"WrongPwd!2026"`.<br>3) `POST /api/auth/login` with that body.<br>4) Assert status is not 2xx, not 5xx, not 404, not 403, and is strictly 401.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | • Register status 200..299 (precondition)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: setup user could not be registered — signals a TC01-level registration bug rather than a login bug; TC05 cannot test its intended scenario.<br>• Login status **strictly 401**<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: any of the four misclassifications below — password check skipped (2xx), unhandled exception (5xx), user-enumeration (404), structurally wrong (403).<br>• NOT 2xx (login must reject; would mean no password check)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: `passwordEncoder.matches()` not called — login service returns a token for any password as long as the email exists (critical security vulnerability).<br>• NOT 5xx (server must handle bcrypt mismatch cleanly)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: `BadCredentialsException` or NPE from `passwordEncoder.matches(null, hash)` propagating unhandled through the service as a 500.<br>• NOT 404 (would leak user-enumeration; should be 401 even when account exists)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: login service throws `UserNotFoundException` for the *wrong password* case — the user **exists** but the password is wrong; returning 404 leaks account presence (OWASP anti-pattern).<br>• NOT 403 (login is the act of obtaining permissions, not exercising them)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: controller maps `BadCredentialsException` to `@ResponseStatus(FORBIDDEN)` — 403 is structurally incorrect; login is not the exercise of a privilege. |

| 7   | TC07 — Missing Authorization header on a non-User CRUD list returns 401 (negative path)                   | `public`, `authentication`                                                            | `GET crudCollectionPath(firstTopLevelNonUserEntity())` with NO Authorization header                                                                  | Verifies that the JWT auth filter blocks anonymous requests on non-User CRUD endpoints. The same endpoint as TC06 is used so the two form a clean A/B: TC06 valid-token → 2xx, TC07 no-token → 401. No DB setup is needed because the test exercises whether anonymous requests are blocked before any controller logic runs. Common bugs caught: missing `OncePerRequestFilter` registration (filter bean not picked up by Spring Security); accidental `.permitAll()` on the target controller's URL patterns; or the filter applied only in certain request contexts (e.g., only POST, not GET). The assertion ladder mirrors TC05's order: not-2xx → not-5xx → not-404 → not-403 → strictly-401.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | 1) Resolve the first top-level non-User entity (same as TC06, e.g., `Provider` for Booking).<br>2) Build the collection path (e.g., `/api/providers`).<br>3) `GET <path>` with **no Authorization header** (`httpGet`, not `httpGetAuth`).<br>4) Assert status is not 2xx, not 5xx, not 404, not 403, and is strictly 401.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | • GET status **strictly 401**<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: auth filter not registered, `.permitAll()` on this URL pattern, or filter has a code path that lets anonymous requests through — complete authentication bypass.<br>• NOT 2xx (endpoint wide-open — critical security bug)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: entire service deployed without authentication; any anonymous caller can read all entity collections.<br>• NOT 5xx (filter chain crashed instead of cleanly rejecting)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: NPE in the filter when the `Authorization` header is absent — student calls `header.substring(7)` without first null-checking the header value.<br>• NOT 404 (endpoint reachable without auth — wrong; auth must block FIRST)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: filter passes the request through; the controller queries an empty table and returns `[]` with 200, or the controller's path is wrong and Spring returns 404 — either way, auth was never checked.<br>• NOT 403 (we sent NO credentials; 403 means "authenticated but lacking permission")<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: student uses `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` without an earlier auth gate; Spring resolves an anonymous principal as "authenticated with no roles" and throws `AccessDeniedException` → 403 instead of 401.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| 8   | TC08 — Tampered JWT signature is rejected with 401 (negative path)                                        | `public`, `authentication`                                                            | `adminToken()` (setup), `GET crudCollectionPath(firstTopLevelNonUserEntity())` with **tampered** Bearer token                                        | Verifies that the auth filter actually validates the JWT signature, not merely decodes the header and payload. `tamperSignature()` preserves the header and payload of a real token (so it looks structurally valid and passes any "3 segments?" check) but replaces the signature segment with a base64 encoding of `"tampered-signature-does-not-verify"`. A correct HMAC-SHA256 filter rejects this because the expected signature over the original payload does not match. The third leg of the auth-filter triad: TC06 valid → 2xx, TC07 none → 401, **TC08 forged → 401**. Critical bug caught: student calls `Jwts.parserBuilder().build().parseClaimsJwt()` (unsigned variant) instead of `parseSignedClaims()`, trusting payload claims without verifying the signature — enabling anyone to edit the payload (e.g., change role to ADMIN) and re-base64 it without detection.                                                                                                          | 1) Call `adminToken()` to get a real, fully-valid admin JWT.<br>2) Call `tamperSignature(token)` — keeps `header.payload` intact but replaces the signature segment with base64(`"tampered-signature-does-not-verify"`).<br>3) Resolve the first top-level non-User entity (same as TC06/TC07, e.g., `Provider` for Booking).<br>4) `GET <collection-path>` with header `Authorization: Bearer <tampered-token>`.<br>5) Assert status is not 2xx, not 5xx, not 404, not 403, and is strictly 401.                                                                                                                                                                                          | • GET status **strictly 401**<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: complete JWT signature bypass — student uses the unsigned parser variant (`parseClaimsJwt()`) or decodes the payload with `Base64.decode()` directly; the tampered token is accepted as valid.<br>• NOT 2xx (signature not actually verified — critical security bug)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: anyone can forge tokens by editing the payload and re-encoding it; privilege escalation to ADMIN by hand-editing the role claim is possible.<br>• NOT 5xx (filter chain crashed instead of cleanly rejecting)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: `JwtException` or `SignatureException` thrown during verification is not caught in the filter's try-catch block, propagating as an unhandled 500 instead of a clean 401.<br>• NOT 404 (signature mismatch must be caught FIRST)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: filter passes the tampered token through to the controller, which queries for a resource; the query returns nothing and the controller returns 404 — auth was never enforced.<br>• NOT 403 (forged = not-authenticated → 401, not 403)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Bug it catches: filter catches the `JwtException` but maps it to `AccessDeniedException` instead of `AuthenticationException`, producing 403 instead of the semantically correct 401.                                                                                                                                                                               |

| 13  | TC13 — Forged role-claim token (payload modified post-signing) is rejected (negative path)                | `public`, `authentication`                                                            | `POST registerPath()` (setup), `POST loginPath()` (setup), `GET crudCollectionPath(firstTopLevelNonUserEntity())` with payload-tampered Bearer token | The signature must cover the payload: modifying the payload while keeping the original signature must invalidate the token. The test obtains a real CUSTOMER JWT, decodes the payload, replaces the role claim with `"ADMIN"` (or injects one if absent), re-base64url-encodes the tampered payload, and reassembles `header.tamperedPayload.originalSignature`. A correct filter — using `Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build().parseSignedClaims()` — rejects this because the stored signature was computed over the *original* payload. Acceptable rejections: 401 (signature failure in the filter) or 403 (signature passes but server re-validates role from DB and finds CUSTOMER).
